title: Rising Temperature
description:
Table `Weather` records the temperature on given dates. `recordDate` is unique.

Write a query to find the `id` of all dates where the temperature was **higher than the previous day** (yesterday — not simply the previous row present in the table).

Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT w.id
FROM Weather w
JOIN Weather prev
  ON DATE(w.recordDate, '-1 day') = prev.recordDate
WHERE w.temperature > prev.temperature;
hint: Join the table to itself on a date offset of one day: DATE(recordDate, '-1 day') in SQLite. LAG() over the rows is not the same thing when dates have gaps.
outputExplanation: January 2 (25°) is warmer than January 1 (10°), and January 4 (30°) is warmer than January 3 (20°). January 3 (20°) is cooler than the day before, and January 6 (40°) has no previous day in the table.

tests.name: Strictly decreasing — no dates are warmer than the previous day
Strictly increasing — every consecutive pair qualifies
Equal temperatures are not a rise
Every date is a gap — LAG over ORDER BY would incorrectly match non-consecutive days
Single row — no previous day exists
Ids not in date order — an id-based join would give wrong results
Across a month boundary — January 31 to February 1
Across a leap day — February 28 to February 29 to March 1
Across a year boundary — December 31 to January 1
Negative temperatures, zeros and duplicates in a longer consecutive run
Long consecutive run of 10 days with multiple rises and drops
Dates all have gaps, temperature always rises — LAG would falsely match all
Rise, drop, then rise again over 4 consecutive days
Stress test with 20 dates, mix of consecutive and gaps, across month boundary
All consecutive, only one day qualifies — at the very end
